q: According to Planck's quantum theory, the energy E of a photon of frequency f is:
x: Light is emitted and absorbed in packets (photons), each with energy E = hf, where h is Planck's constant. Energy is directly proportional to frequency.

q: The photoelectric effect is the emission of:
o: Light from a metal surface when it is heated strongly
Protons from a metal surface when light falls on it
Electrons from a metal surface when it is heated strongly
Electrons from a metal surface when light of suitable frequency falls on it
x: In the photoelectric effect, light (photons) of high enough frequency ejects electrons, called photoelectrons, from a metal surface. Emission of electrons by heating is thermionic emission, a different process.

q: The SI unit of Planck's constant h is:
x: h = E/f, so its unit is joule ÷ hertz = J ÷ s⁻¹ = J s. J s⁻¹ is the watt, and N m is the joule.

q: The threshold frequency of a metal is:
o: The minimum frequency of light that can eject electrons from it
The frequency at which the largest number of electrons is ejected
The maximum frequency of light that can eject electrons from it
The frequency at which the photoelectric current becomes saturated
x: Below the threshold frequency no electrons are emitted, however bright the light. Above it, emission occurs and any higher frequency also works, so it is a minimum, not a maximum.

q: In terms of its wavelength λ, the energy of a photon is:
x: Since c = fλ, f = c/λ, and E = hf = hc/λ. Photon energy is inversely proportional to wavelength.

q: The work function of a metal is:
o: The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from its surface
The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons emitted
The energy of each photon falling on the surface
The total energy of all the free electrons in the metal
x: The work function φ is the least energy an electron needs to escape from the metal surface. A photon must supply at least this energy; any extra appears as kinetic energy of the electron.

q: What is the energy of a photon of frequency 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz? (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)
x: E = hf = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ × 5 × 10¹⁴ = 33 × 10⁻²⁰ = 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Dividing h by f instead gives the meaningless 1.3 × 10⁻⁴⁸.

q: The work function φ of a metal and its threshold frequency f₀ are related by:
x: At the threshold frequency the photon has just enough energy to free an electron with zero kinetic energy, so hf₀ = φ.

q: What is the energy of a photon of wavelength 660 nm? (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
x: E = hc/λ = (6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3 × 10⁸) ÷ (6.6 × 10⁻⁷) = 3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Forgetting to convert nm to metres gives 3 × 10⁻²⁸ J; 2 × 10⁻²⁵ J is just hc.

q: Einstein's photoelectric equation, with φ the work function and ½mv²max the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons, is:
x: Each photon gives all its energy hf to one electron: part (φ) is used to escape the surface and the rest is the electron's maximum kinetic energy.

q: If the wavelength of light is halved, the energy of each of its photons:
x: E = hc/λ, so E is inversely proportional to λ. Halving λ doubles the photon energy.

q: Light of a fixed frequency above the threshold falls on a metal. If the intensity of the light is increased, then:
o: The same number of photoelectrons is emitted, but with greater maximum kinetic energy
More photoelectrons are emitted, each with greater maximum kinetic energy
Neither the number nor the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons changes
More photoelectrons are emitted per second, but their maximum kinetic energy is unchanged
x: Higher intensity means more photons per second, so more electrons are ejected. Each photon still has energy hf, so the maximum kinetic energy hf − φ stays the same.

q: Which of these photons carries the most energy?
x: Photon energy E = hf increases with frequency. Of these, violet light has the highest frequency (shortest wavelength), so its photons have the most energy.

q: Light above the threshold frequency falls on a metal. If its frequency is increased, the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons:
x: Maximum kinetic energy = hf − φ. With φ fixed for the metal, a larger f gives a larger maximum kinetic energy.

q: A photon has an energy of 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. What is its energy in electronvolts? (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)
x: Energy in eV = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ ÷ 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 3 eV. Dividing the wrong way round gives 0.33 eV.

q: Very bright red light falls on a metal whose threshold frequency is higher than the frequency of red light. What happens?
o: No electrons are emitted at all
Electrons are emitted only after a time delay
A few fast electrons are emitted
x: Each red photon has less energy than the work function, so it cannot free an electron, however many photons arrive. Intensity cannot make up for a frequency below the threshold.

q: Which statement about photons is correct?
o: They have the same rest mass as an electron
They travel at the speed of light in a vacuum and have zero rest mass
They carry a negative electric charge
The energy of each photon depends on the intensity of the light
x: A photon is a packet of electromagnetic energy: uncharged, with zero rest mass, moving at c in a vacuum. Its energy depends only on frequency (E = hf), not on intensity.

q: Photons of energy 5 eV fall on a metal whose work function is 2 eV. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons?
x: K.E.max = hf − φ = 5 − 2 = 3 eV. Adding the work function instead of subtracting it gives 7 eV.

q: A lamp emits 3.3 W of light, all of frequency 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz. How many photons does it emit per second? (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)
x: Energy of one photon = hf = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ × 5 × 10¹⁴ = 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Photons per second = 3.3 J s⁻¹ ÷ 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 1 × 10¹⁹.

q: A metal has a work function of 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. What is its threshold frequency? (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)
x: f₀ = φ/h = 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ ÷ 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ = 0.5 × 10¹⁵ = 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Dividing h by φ gives 2 × 10⁻¹⁵, and multiplying them gives 2.2 × 10⁻⁵².

q: In the Compton effect an X-ray photon is scattered by a loosely bound electron. Compared with the incident photon, the scattered photon has:
o: A shorter wavelength and more energy
The same wavelength but less speed
A longer wavelength and less energy
The same energy but a different direction only
x: The photon gives part of its energy to the recoiling electron, so its energy E = hc/λ falls and its wavelength increases. Its speed stays c, so a change of speed is the tempting but wrong idea.

q: For an electron, h/m₀c = 2.4 × 10⁻¹² m. An X-ray photon is Compton-scattered by a free electron through an angle of 60°. The increase in its wavelength is:
x: Δλ = (h/m₀c)(1 − cos θ) = 2.4 × 10⁻¹² × (1 − 0.5) = 1.2 × 10⁻¹² m. Using (1 + cos θ) gives 3.6 × 10⁻¹² m; 2.4 and 4.8 × 10⁻¹² m are the shifts at 90° and 180°.

q: The Compton shift Δλ = (h/m₀c)(1 − cos θ) for photons scattered by free electrons does NOT depend on:
o: The rest mass of the scattering particle
The wavelength of the incident photon
x: The formula contains h, m₀, c and θ but not the incident wavelength, so photons of any wavelength scattered through the same angle get the same shift. It is noticed mainly for X-rays because there Δλ is a sizeable fraction of λ.

q: A photon of wavelength 2.4 × 10⁻¹² m is scattered straight back (θ = 180°) by a free electron. For an electron, h/m₀c = 2.4 × 10⁻¹² m. What fraction of the photon's energy is given to the electron?
x: Δλ = 2.4 × 10⁻¹² × (1 − cos 180°) = 4.8 × 10⁻¹² m, so λ' = 7.2 × 10⁻¹² m = 3λ and the photon keeps E/3. The electron gets 1 − 1/3 = 2/3. Using the 90° shift gives 1/2; 1/3 is the photon's share, not the electron's.

q: The rest-mass energy of an electron is 0.51 MeV. The minimum energy a photon must have to produce an electron-positron pair is:
x: Pair production creates two particles, each of rest energy m₀c² = 0.51 MeV, so the photon needs at least 2 × 0.51 = 1.02 MeV. Forgetting the positron gives 0.51 MeV.

q: A gamma-ray photon of energy 3.02 MeV produces an electron-positron pair near a nucleus. The rest-mass energy of an electron is 0.51 MeV. The total kinetic energy of the electron and positron is:
x: Energy used to create the pair = 2 × 0.51 = 1.02 MeV, so the kinetic energy shared by the two is 3.02 − 1.02 = 2.00 MeV. Subtracting only one rest energy gives 2.51 MeV; 1.00 MeV is each particle's share if split equally.

q: An electron and a positron, both nearly at rest, annihilate and produce two identical photons. For an electron, h/m₀c = 2.4 × 10⁻¹² m. The wavelength of each photon is:
x: The total energy 2m₀c² is shared by two photons, so each has E = m₀c² and λ = hc/E = hc/(m₀c²) = h/m₀c = 2.4 × 10⁻¹² m. Giving all 2m₀c² to one photon gives 1.2 × 10⁻¹² m; two photons are needed so that momentum stays zero.

q: The de Broglie wavelength of a particle of mass m moving with speed v is:
x: de Broglie proposed λ = h/p, and p = mv for a slow particle, so λ = h/(mv). A larger momentum means a shorter wavelength; the other forms have the wrong units.

q: The speed of a particle (well below the speed of light) is doubled. Its de Broglie wavelength:
x: λ = h/(mv), so λ ∝ 1/v and doubling v halves λ. One quarter is the slip of treating λ as depending on v² (as kinetic energy does).

q: A particle of mass 6.63 × 10⁻²⁷ kg moves at 1 × 10³ m s⁻¹. What is its de Broglie wavelength? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)
x: p = mv = 6.63 × 10⁻²⁷ × 10³ = 6.63 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹, so λ = h/p = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/6.63 × 10⁻²⁴ = 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Dividing by the mass but forgetting the speed gives 1 × 10⁻⁷ m; multiplying by the speed instead gives 1 × 10⁻⁴ m.

q: An electron starting from rest is accelerated through a potential difference V. If V is made four times larger, the electron's de Broglie wavelength becomes:
x: eV = p²/2m gives p = √(2meV), so λ = h/√(2meV) ∝ 1/√V. Four times the voltage gives √4 = 2 times the momentum and half the wavelength. Forgetting the square root gives one quarter.

q: A proton and an alpha particle, both starting from rest, are accelerated through the same potential difference. Take the alpha particle's mass as 4 times and its charge as 2 times the proton's. The ratio (proton's de Broglie wavelength)/(alpha particle's wavelength) is:
x: qV = p²/2m gives λ = h/√(2mqV) ∝ 1/√(mq). The ratio is √(m_α q_α/m_p q_p) = √(4 × 2) = √8 = 2√2. Using the masses only gives 2; forgetting the square root on the mass ratio gives 4.

q: An electron microscope can show much finer detail than an optical microscope mainly because:
o: Electrons have no mass and are not diffracted
The de Broglie wavelength of fast electrons is much shorter than that of visible light
Electron lenses magnify more than glass lenses can
x: Resolving power improves as the wavelength gets shorter; electrons accelerated through a few kilovolts have wavelengths thousands of times shorter than visible light. Electrons are slower than light and do have mass, so those options are false.

q: A beam of electrons passing through a thin crystal produces a pattern of rings on a screen, like the pattern of X-rays. This shows that electrons:
o: Have a definite position at every instant
Travel at the speed of light
x: Diffraction rings are a wave effect, so electron diffraction confirms de Broglie's idea that moving particles have a wavelength. The charge of the electron plays no role in forming the rings.

q: According to Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, which pair of quantities cannot both be measured exactly at the same time for a particle?
x: The principle says Δx Δp is at least of the order of h, so making one more precise makes the other less precise. The same holds for energy and time (ΔE Δt), not for mass and charge.

q: The position of an electron is known to within 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Using Δx Δp ≈ h with h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, the uncertainty in its momentum is about:
x: Δp ≈ h/Δx = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/10⁻¹⁰ = 6.63 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹. Multiplying by Δx instead of dividing gives 6.63 × 10⁻⁴⁴, and inverting h/Δx gives about 1.5 × 10²³.

q: An electron is confined to a region 1 × 10⁻⁹ m wide. Using Δx Δp ≈ h, the uncertainty in its speed is about: (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg)
x: Δp ≈ h/Δx = 6.63 × 10⁻²⁵ kg m s⁻¹, so Δv = Δp/m = 6.63 × 10⁻²⁵/9.1 × 10⁻³¹ ≈ 0.73 × 10⁶ = 7.3 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. 7.3 × 10⁶ comes from using 10⁻¹⁰ m for the width; 1.4 × 10⁻⁶ is m/Δp, the ratio upside down.

q: The uncertainty in the position of a particle is halved. According to the uncertainty principle, the minimum uncertainty in its momentum:
x: Δx Δp ≈ constant, so Δp ∝ 1/Δx; halving Δx doubles the least Δp. 'Halves' treats them as proportional, and 'four times' wrongly squares the factor.

q: An atom stays in an excited state for about 1 × 10⁻⁸ s. Using ΔE Δt ≈ h with h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, the uncertainty in the energy of that state is about:
x: ΔE ≈ h/Δt = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/10⁻⁸ = 6.63 × 10⁻²⁶ J. Multiplying by Δt gives 6.63 × 10⁻⁴², and inverting the ratio gives about 1.5 × 10²⁵ J.

q: Suppose an electron were confined inside a nucleus of size 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. Using Δx Δp ≈ h and taking its energy as E ≈ pc, its energy would be about: (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
x: p ≈ h/Δx = 6.63 × 10⁻²⁰ kg m s⁻¹, so E ≈ pc = 6.63 × 10⁻²⁰ × 3 × 10⁸ ≈ 2 × 10⁻¹¹ J (about 120 MeV), far more than nuclear beta energies, so electrons cannot live inside the nucleus. 6.6 × 10⁻²⁰ is the momentum value, forgetting to multiply by c.
